extraction.research_question: Do special-interest groups (mainly publicly traded firms, their corporate PACs and their employees) donate to members of Congress whom they later lobby on related bills? The paper tests a sequential "access-buying" link: a first-time donation to a politician is followed by lobbying on bills sponsored by, co-sponsored by, or assigned to committees of that same politician.
extraction.theory: Access-buying hypothesis: donations secure access to legislators, and lobbying then informs them or shapes content (pp.5-6). Alternatives discussed: electoral and ideological motives (Poole and Romer 1985); legislative subsidy (Hall and Deardorff 2006); donations as rewards after favorable action (Snyder 1990, tested in App.K). Three hypotheses (pp.6-8): (H1) donors lobby bills the politician sponsors; (H2) donors lobby bills the politician co-sponsors; (H3) donors lobby bills assigned to the politician's committees, the strongest link expected. Corporate PAC donations are expected to show a stronger link than employee or CEO donations.
extraction.data: Main sample: publicly traded US manufacturing firms (NAICS 2-digit 31-33) and all members of Congress serving 2008-2018 (979 members, 2,703 firms). Unbalanced panel of 2,646,237 firm-politician dyads and 16,428,834 observations per text (p.15). Table 1 and App. H report N = 16,434,912, which does not match the text; flagged in limitations. Unit: firm-politician-year dyad. Lobbying source: LDA reports, over 1.2 million parsed, of which 1.27 million (1999-2020) are cited, with 0.25 million (about 20%) mentioning specific bills and covering about 97% of lobbying spending (pp.9-10). Donation source: FEC filings, over 75 million records since 1999 (abstract and p.11); about 53 million itemized individual contributions 1980-2018 (p.11). Interest-group coverage: over 84,000 groups (abstract; p.2). Other samples: 2013 cross-section of all public firms (9,791 firms, 597 members, 5,845,227 possible dyads; App.D); services firms (App.H.2, NAICS 42-81); 1999-2000 interest-group comparison (App.G); 111th Congress (2009-2010) Senate miscellaneous tariff bills (MTBs), 477 bills and 107 lobbying firms (App.L). Covariates from Volden and Wiseman (2018) and Compustat (sales, employees).
extraction.method: (1) Linear probability model with fixed effects (Eq. 2, Table 1, App.H). Outcome: firm lobbies a bill tied to politician j in year t through sponsorship, co-sponsorship or committee. Treatment: first-time donation within a 3-year window (Eq. 1, L=3). Fixed-effect structures vary across columns: firm, year, politician, and firm-politician. Standard errors clustered by firm. (2) Difference-in-differences with matching (Eqs. 3-4, Figs. 4-5, Tables J.1-J.3). Each treated pair (i,j) with a first-time donation in t is matched to 10 nearest firms (Mahalanobis distance on sales, employees and lobbying up to t-1) that gave j no donation in t to t-3. Estimand: change from t-1 to t+F in the lobbying outcome, treated minus matched-control mean, averaged over treated pairs. 95% CIs from block bootstrap. Robustness: NAICS 3-digit matching (Table J.2), donor-type splits (Fig.5), lagged donations (Table H.5), lobbying-to-donation reverse test (App.K, Table K.1). (3) Descriptive comparisons with Ansolabehere, Snyder and Tripathi (2002) (App.D, E, G).
extraction.identification: Within-politician comparison. Variation is across firm-politician pairs with the same politician, so politician-specific productivity and ideology are absorbed (p.2). The first-time-donation-in-3-years design separates new donations from ongoing ones and makes donation timing identifiable. The DiD assumes parallel trends: the matched controls' pre-period lagged outcome changes are constant (p.24). Covariate balance improves after Mahalanobis matching (App.I). Firm-politician alignment is handled by firm-politician FE (cols 4 and 8 of Table 1). Unobserved firm-politician-time shocks are not handled, and the authors say the estimates are not causal (pp.28-29).
extraction.scope: Population: publicly traded US manufacturing firms (services and all-public-firm checks in appendices), lobbying and PAC/employee donations to members of Congress. Institution: US federal Congress (House and Senate), with lobbying under LDA and donations under FECA. Era: main analysis 2008-2018 (LDA electronic filing mandatory after the 2007 HLOGA amendment, p.15); descriptive work 1999-2020; the 1999-2000 comparison uses interest-group data. Results are observational and do not establish causation.

key_findings.finding: Firm-politician Table 1 OLS: a first-time donation within 3 years raises the probability that the firm lobbies a bill tied to the politician (sponsor, co-sponsor or committee) by 2.3 to 4.8 percentage points. Base rate of such lobbying is about 0.07.
key_findings.location: Table 1 and text, pp.19-20; FE-heavy col.4 coefficient 0.023

key_findings.finding: Matched DiD: donations raise the probability of lobbying a politician-linked bill, rising over time. Senate effect is about 8 pp at t+0, rising to about 11 pp at t+3; the House effect is larger.
key_findings.location: Figure 4, pp.25-26; Table J.1, p.17; text p.26
key_findings.numbers: Senate: 0.075, 0.097, 0.108, 0.110 (t+0 to t+3); House: 0.086, 0.111, 0.127, 0.127; Senate SE about 0.003-0.004, House SE about 0.002-0.003; 3,778 Senate and 5,497 House first-time donation instances

key_findings.finding: Corporate PAC donations show the strongest link to later lobbying, especially committee-related lobbying. Employee and CEO donations also show links, but smaller ones.
key_findings.numbers: Committee lobbying, PAC: 0.103 (t+0) rising to 0.147 (t+3); CEO 0.017 to 0.050; Employee 0.015 to 0.039. Sponsorship, PAC: 0.029 to 0.037; CEO 0.012 to 0.029; Employee 0.014 to 0.022. Co-sponsorship, PAC: 0.097 to 0.102. Table J.3 CEO co-sponsorship at t+2 is 0.28, which is far above the rest of its row and is not discussed in the text. Instance counts: PAC 2,662; CEO 792; Employee 934

key_findings.finding: Donations are followed by lobbying, not the reverse. Lobbying does not raise later donations, except a small effect of lobbying a bill's sponsor at t+0.
key_findings.location: Appendix K, Figure K.1, Table K.1, p.20-21 (text p.26)
key_findings.numbers: Lobby Sponsor t+0 coef 0.0074 (SE 0.0028); other lags and types near zero; 12,232,896 firm-politician-quarter dyads; lobby-sponsor instances 4,426

key_findings.finding: Donations and lobbying are concentrated. About 5% of public firms both donate and lobby, and they account for most political spending.
key_findings.location: Data section p.5; Table D.1, p.4 and p.6; App.D
key_findings.numbers: 2013: 518 of 9,791 public firms (5%) both donate and lobby, responsible for $2.6bn of $2.86bn (89%). Firm-politician dyads with both: 12,862 (less than 0.1% of 5,845,227) containing $520m (18%). About 4% of all dyads have any political link

key_findings.finding: Among firms that both lobby and donate, PAC donations and lobbying spending are positively and significantly associated (log-log).
key_findings.numbers: beta = 0.88, R2 = 0.39; text: a 10% PAC increase is associated with 8.8% more lobbying among firms that also lobby

key_findings.finding: Most donation-only links come from employees, not corporate PACs.
key_findings.numbers: 19,735 of 23,270 donation-only dyads in 2013 (about 85%) are created by employee donations

key_findings.finding: Miscellaneous tariff bills (MTBs), a descriptive success check: firms that lobby and donate to the senator from their state or to Senate Finance members see MTB approval more often than lobby-only firms. The paper calls the gap significant, but no test is reported.
key_findings.location: Appendix L, Table L.1 (duplicated as L.2), pp.24-26
key_findings.numbers: Lobby-only: 23 of 66 (0.348) approved. Lobby+donate: 17 of 41 (0.415). Difference 0.067 (+19%). 477 Senate MTBs in 111th Congress; 211 proposed by 46 public firms; 107 public firms lobbied on MTBs

key_findings.finding: Heterogeneity by the dyad and group of interest: the paper says the donation-lobbying link is strongest for corporations, weaker for labor unions; this replicates Ansolabehere et al. (2002) using 1999-2000 data.
key_findings.numbers: Beta (cube-root PAC vs lobbying): corporations 2.0; membership organizations 1.6; trade associations 0.8; labor unions 0.6; no relationship for unions per text

limitations: Not causal. The authors say their estimates should not be read as causal and that the study shows an association (pp.3, 28-29). Donation timing may be driven by unobserved firm-politician-time shocks.
Lobbying is measured only through bill-linked reports: about 20% of 1.27 million reports cite bills. The authors call the results a lower bound (p.10).
Bill positions are reported for only about 17% of lobbied bills; 82% of those are supportive (fn.12, p.17).
Parallel trends are assumed; the authors check only that the lagged-outcome difference is roughly constant (p.24). Matching uses sales, employees and lobbying up to t-1 only.

Sample inconsistencies: text says 16,428,834 observations, while Table 1 and App. H report 16,434,912. The donation-amount effect is stated as 0.03 pp per 10%, which matches only the firm-politician-FE column (0.003), not col.5 (0.006).

Lobbying data quality: LDA reports lack unique bill IDs, reporting changed from semi-annual to quarterly in 2008, and the sample starts in 2008 for these reasons (fns.5, 9; p.15). Bill matching relies on cross-referencing bill numbers and titles.

Relationships may reflect the revolving door or association lobbying; lobbyists with covered positions are about 7.8% of lobbyists and their lobbying on sponsored bills is under 1% (fn.15). The authors argue this does not drive results.
Manufacturing focus: service firms give almost identical results (App.H.2). Donor types are correlated (p.27), so type-specific effects are not independent.

MTB analysis is one Congress (111th), descriptive, and small (41 vs 66 firms). No significance test is reported despite the word 'significant' on p.25. Table L.2 duplicates Table L.1 in the extraction.

Unit of donation treatment is first-time donation within 3 years; the authors note that first-time-ever donations give almost identical results (App.H.3-H.5), but this is not a test of a different identification.
measures: Outcome: binary firm-politician-year indicator that the firm lobbies a bill sponsored by, co-sponsored by, or assigned to a committee of politician j (Y^a_ijt, with a in {Sponsor, Co-sponsor, Committee}).
Treatment: first-time donation within 3 years (X*_ijt(L), L=3), and logged first-time donation amount.
Donor types: corporate PAC (PAC $), CEO/executive, and rank-and-file employee donations; government-relations staff donations used in App.E.
Lobbying spending: Lobby $ allocated across bills and politicians (App.C, a noisy measure; binary link used in main analysis).
Politician controls: party, majority status, committee chair, membership of top-4 powerful committees (Groseclose-Stewart scores), from Volden and Wiseman (2018).
Firm controls: sales and employees (Compustat); matching covariates: sales, employees, lobbying up to t-1 (Mahalanobis distance, 10 nearest).
Occupation codes: SOC 11-1011 (executives) and 27-3030 (public relations/government affairs) to classify employees; name matching via graph clustering and fastLink (Enamorado, Fifield and Imai 2019).

summary_md:
Kim, Stuckatz and Wolters build a firm-politician-year panel. It covers 2,703 publicly traded manufacturing firms and 979 members of Congress from 2008 to 2018. Lobbying comes from parsed LDA reports that name bills, and donations come from FEC records. The question is whether a firm's first donation to a member in a 3-year window is followed by the firm lobbying bills that the member sponsors, co-sponsors, or that go to the member's committees.

**Fixed-effects results.** The models compare firm-politician pairs within the same politician. A new donation goes with a 2.3 to 4.8 percentage-point higher chance of that lobbying. The base rate is about 0.07. These are pooled estimates (UNSTRATIFIED by chamber or donor type).

**Matched difference-in-differences.** These results are split by chamber. Senate estimates rise from 7.5 pp at t+0 to 11 pp at t+3. House estimates rise from 8.6 to 12.7 pp.

**Donor type and channel.** The link is strongest for corporate PAC money and for lobbying tied to committees. For PACs, committee-linked lobbying rises from 0.103 to 0.147. CEO and employee donations show much weaker links, and lobbying does not predict later donations. Only about 5% of public firms both donate and lobby (2013).

**Limits.** The authors say plainly that the results are associations, not causal effects. The lobbying measure reaches the member only through who sponsors the bill or which committee gets it, because LDA filings never name members.

**What it means for Melange.**
- It is the closest published counterpart to the closed FEC x LDA bridge test. The paper uses a different unit (firm-member pairs over time, not a member-level cross-section) and different fixed effects.
- It also points to a gap. The paper's strongest channel, committee referral, is missing from the system's LobbyView outcome, which counts only sponsor and cosponsor links. And the system's own committee control may absorb that channel.
- It supports the engine's choice to measure money from direct PACs only, and the "money buys access" stance as a weak prior. It does not speak to votes or flips.

All of this is UNVERIFIED agent analysis until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Within-politician, first-time-donation designs find donations followed by lobbying on the member's bills: Table 1 coefs 0.023-0.048 (pooled, UNSTRATIFIED, N=16.4M firm-politician-years, 2008-2018); matched DiD Senate 0.075->0.110, House 0.086->0.127 (t+0..t+3; 3,778 Senate / 5,497 House instances). The committee channel is strongest (PAC committee 0.103->0.147 vs sponsorship 0.029->0.037). Lobbying does not predict later donations (App. K).
bearings.paper_location: Table 1 pp.19-20; Fig.4 and Table J.1 pp.25-26; Fig.5 and Table J.3 p.27; App. K
bearings.system_side: Bridge round 3 is a member-level cross-sectional correlation (Spearman). X is a member's FEC exposure for each industry and cycle. Y is LobbyView n_bills: lobbied bills the member sponsored or cosponsored, for 22 lob_ids in CU, fintech and crypto, 2023-26. Four controls: party, chamber, volume and committee. Raw rho +0.153; four-control partial -0.0002. Verdict UNCORROBORATED, route CLOSED for this window. The prereg itself already names an overcontrol reading: 'association present but not separable from committee structure'.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's unit is the firm-member pair over time, with politician, firm and pair fixed effects and first-time donation timing. That design tests a different estimand from a member-level cross-section with a committee control. Because the paper finds the association runs mainly through committee-linked bills, the bridge's committee control plausibly absorbs the very channel the paper measures. So the round-3 null and the paper's positive estimates are not in conflict. Sample mismatch: the paper covers about 2,700 manufacturing firms in 2008-2018; the bridge covers 22 financial-sector clients in 2023-26. The paper is not causal either. Per the prereg, this cannot license re-running the bridge on the same window with different controls. It informs only a successor prereg on a new LobbyView vintage.

bearings.paper_claim: The outcome is a firm lobbying any bill tied to politician j through sponsorship, co-sponsorship or committee referral. Bills are matched by number and title, because LDA reports carry no member names and no unique bill IDs. Only about 20% of 1.27M reports cite bills; the authors call the results a lower bound.
bearings.paper_location: Eq.2 and pp.9-11, fn.5, fn.9, p.15
bearings.system_side: The member link is built by joining each lobbied bill to its sponsor/cosponsor roster ('did this organization lobby a bill this member sponsored or cosponsored'). P(joined | lobbied) = 1 by construction, so the link is REFUTED as evidence of influence or contact.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's outcome is the same roster-join construction, plus a committee-referral arm. It escapes the system's circularity only because its treatment is donation timing, not bill joining. It is still a measure of a member's involvement in lobbied bills, not of contact with the member. That matches the system's ruling that the join is not a contact measure. It gives no license to use the join as an influence edge (D-021). It does show a coverage gap: the system's roster has no committee-referral link.

bearings.paper_claim: Corporate PAC donations show the strongest sequential association with later lobbying of the recipient: committee lobbying 0.103->0.147, versus CEO 0.017->0.050 and employee 0.015->0.039. The authors frame this as consistent with access-buying. They state 'our estimates should not be interpreted as causal' (p.29). The amount effect is small (0.003 per 10% in the firm-politician FE column).
bearings.paper_location: Fig.5 and Table J.3 p.27; Table 1 col.4; pp.28-29
bearings.system_side: WM 0.35 / WP 0.65 is calibrated on the premise that money buys access and effort more than votes. Engine money comes only from direct PAC contributions (Schedule B 24K/24Z); individual contributions are out of scope. The money term is a saturating function of the amount relative to receipts, with no timing or first-donation feature.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper backs the 'money is about access' premise and the PAC-only scope: PAC money is the channel with the strongest association. It says nothing about roll-call flips, the quantity pflip models. Its outcome is the firm's lobbying behaviour, not the member's position. Sample is manufacturing firms 2008-2018, not CU or bank PACs. The evidence is associative. Treat it as a weak prior for the WM<WP choice, not an estimate of WM.

bearings.paper_claim: Of the three links (sponsor, co-sponsor, committee), committee-linked lobbying after a donation is the largest and grows over time (PAC 0.103->0.147, t+0..t+3). H3 predicts this because bills pass through committees; chair status enters only as a control.
bearings.paper_location: Hypotheses pp.6-8; Fig.5 p.27; Table J.3
bearings.system_side: Influence% = committee_raw/max, built from seat weights by CU-relevance tier (Highly 3.0 / Moderately 1.8 / Slightly 0.9, subcommittee 1/6) and leadership multipliers (Chair 3.0 full / 7.5 sub; Ranking 2.0 / 4.5).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports the claim that interest groups concentrate money and lobbying on committee members. That is evidence that committee position is a structural target layer, in line with Paul's position. It does not estimate the chair/ranking ladder, the 1/6 subcommittee weight, or committee effects on CU bill outcomes. It shows where firms act, not whose action moves bills. Sample is manufacturing firms at federal level, 2008-2018.

bearings.paper_claim: Individual FEC donors are linked to firms and to Govtrack/FEC candidate IDs through constrained graph clustering and fastLink probabilistic record linkage (Enamorado, Fifield and Imai 2019). Executives and government-relations staff are classified with SOC occupation codes 11-1011 and 27-3030.
bearings.paper_location: Data section pp.11-12; Measures (SOC codes)
bearings.system_side: Same-name donor candidates are resolved by an ordered rule ladder: exact name + zip -> AUTO; cross-employer -> HIGH; nickname/same city, state + occupation and employer contradiction -> REVIEW; otherwise DISCARD. There is no name-frequency weighting.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Directly relevant: both systems face the same FEC problem of donors with no unique identifier. fastLink's frequency-weighted match scores would address the ladder's known blind spot, which is that common names in the same zip get AUTO. The paper reports no precision or recall for its linkage, so it offers a method, not a benchmark. Mentat's strict-names and exclude-on-contradiction rulings (D-040) still govern; any change is Paul's call.

gaps_exposed: The system's LobbyView member outcome (lob_id x bioguide x year n_bills) links members only as sponsor or cosponsor of a lobbied bill. It has no committee-referral arm, which is the channel where the paper's association is largest. Brain note lobbyview-collector.md:127 confirms edges = sponsor + all cosponsors.

No org x member panel over time: the bridge is a member-level cross-section with a committee control. Nothing in the system can separate a relationship's onset (a first donation) from continued giving, so the paper's within-politician, first-time-donation design has no counterpart.

Engine money features (flip_model, money_response) are amounts per two-year cycle relative to receipts. They have no timing or relationship-onset signal, even though the paper finds the binary first-donation indicator carries the association and the amount effect is small.
No reverse-direction check (lobbying followed by donations) exists alongside the bridge. The paper treats that check as a key way to rule out reverse causation (App. K).
flags: D-021: the paper builds a firm-politician bipartite graph from LDA bill mentions joined to sponsor, co-sponsor and committee rosters (Fig.1, App.F). Adopting those links as Melange edges or weights would breach D-021 (LDA is an identity source only) and reproduce the circular roster join (lobby_interactions.py:4).

Wording (D-025 family): 'access-buying' is the authors' hypothesis; the results are associations ('not causal', pp.3, 29). No figure from this paper may be presented as an access, closeness or introduction probability, or as donations causing lobbying.

Pooled-coefficient rule: Table 1's 2.3-4.8 pp estimates pool House and Senate and all donor types; quote them as UNSTRATIFIED (window 2008-2018, denominator 16.4M firm-politician-years). The chamber-stratified DiD (Senate 0.075-0.110, House 0.086-0.127) is the stratified figure.

Paper-internal inconsistencies: the text says N=16,428,834 while Table 1 and App.H report 16,434,912. Table J.3 has a CEO co-sponsorship value of 0.28 at t+2, out of line with its row. App. L calls the MTB gap (0.415 vs 0.348; 41 vs 66 firms) 'significant' without reporting a test.
Bridge closure: the round-3 prereg bars a different control set on the 2023-26 window as a successor. This paper supports only a successor prereg on a new LobbyView vintage, never a re-run.

Paul's media-blend note says Kim's effects fade within 2 to 3 years. This 2023 version shows estimates rising from t+0 to t+3 and stopping at t+3; it does not measure any fade. The note should not be used as a decay timescale for press/social half-lives or staffer-tie decay.
Neither rejected SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization) is argued in this paper.
All bearings are new agent analysis and stay UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces them (DE-062).
paul_alignment: The paper agrees with Paul's core expectation that donations precede lobbying. It does so at the firm-member level, within the same politician, and as an association only. It is also consistent with Furnas's low overlap: only about 5% of public firms both donate and lobby. The system's closed bridge null does not contradict the paper. That test uses a member-level cross-section with a committee control, a different unit and possibly an overcontrol of the paper's strongest channel. Paul's notes do not record this distinction. His committee-pillar position (money and lobbying effects strongest in committee activity) is supported in direction. The paper says nothing about the pillar's weights. His annotation for media-blend and access-uncertainty, that Kim's effects fade within 2 to 3 years, is stale or inaccurate for this version: the estimates rise through t+3 and no fade is measured. The annotation names this work as JOP 2026; the PDF read here is a December 2023 working version, and the journal and DOI are not confirmed in the text.

related.why: An earlier working version of the same project, with the same authors, data and first-time-donation design. This 2023 version adds the matched DiD and the appendices.

Furnas finds low overlap between organizational lobbying and PAC spending. This paper's 2013 figure, 518 of 9,791 public firms (5%) doing both, is consistent with that, and its sequential finding applies only within that overlap.
A randomized field experiment on whether contributions open access. This paper cites it (p.4) as the closest causal benchmark for its observational access-buying association.
LobbyView's firm-level bill-linked LDA parsing is the lobbying source here. It is also the source of the system's lob_id network and its bridge outcome.
Imai and Kim's cautions on two-way fixed effects and matched DiD apply directly to this paper's FE LPM and matched DiD, and to any successor design for the bridge.
This paper has bill positions for only about 17% of lobbied bills. Kim 2025's LLM-derived positions on the same LobbyView data would let a donation-lobbying link be signed by support or opposition.
The same LobbyView firm-politician bipartite construction from bill sponsorship, used for community detection instead of sequential timing.
Cited (pp.28-29) as evidence on firm-level returns to lobbying. It shares the In Song Kim lineage and LobbyView firm data.
A review of empirical lobbying models that places the access-buying and legislative-subsidy mechanisms this paper weighs.

extraction.research_question: Can an interest group obtain superior access to senior congressional officials because its members have donated to political campaigns? Put as a counterfactual: would House offices have treated the same group members differently had the offices not known they were donors? (p.545, p.548)
extraction.theory: Campaign contributions may buy access through quid pro quo exchange, expected future donations, forestalling donations to rivals, and signals of ideology, expertise or preference intensity; access is a precondition for influence and legislators' time is finite. Observational work is confounded by shared ideology, and contributors may give to legislators who already support them or to those whose support is in doubt. (pp.546-548)
extraction.data: Unit: congressional office (district scheduler contacted by e-mail). Sample: every U.S. House representative of one party who had not already cosponsored the bill, 191 offices after one of an original 192 was dropped because of a misdirected e-mail (fn 5, p.549). Recruited attendees: around a dozen CREDO Action members per district who had previously donated to campaigns (p.549). Organization: CREDO Action, a liberal political organization with about 3.5 million members (p.549). Period: implementation June, July and August 2013 (p.551). Bill: a measure to ban a chemical; no vote was held (p.549, p.554). Per-arm counts are not reported in the text; the design implies 64 Revealed Donor offices (one per block) and 127 Constituent offices, which matches the Table 1 percentages (derived, not stated). Party is not named in the text.
extraction.method: Blocked randomized field experiment. Offices were blocked into 64 triplets using blockTools (Mahalanobis distance) on six covariates; one office per block randomly assigned to Revealed Donor and two to Constituent (pp.549-550). The request e-mail described attendees as "local campaign donors" (Revealed Donor) or "local constituents" (Constituent); nothing else varied, and correspondence was standardized by a prespecified protocol (pp.550-551). Outcome: the rank of the official who would attend, recorded more than 24 hours in advance and confirmed after the meeting, coded into six ordered categories by two coders blind to assignment (p.552). Analysis: exact p-values from randomization inference under the sharp null, one comparison per cumulative rank; Bonferroni check across five comparisons; ordered probit with randomization-inference p-value as an omnibus test (pp.552-554).
extraction.identification: Identification rests on random assignment of offices to the donor-label versus constituent-label condition, within covariate blocks, so covariates (balance omnibus p=.92, chi-square 1.44, 5 df, p.550) and chance differences in official availability are balanced by design. The randomized treatment is the donor status of attendees as revealed to the office, not actual contributions; this is a "mechanism experiment" that approximates randomizing donor status (fn 4, p.548). Donors' actual giving was not randomized and no deception occurred: the meetings were real, attendees knew donations might be disclosed, and the requests asked for nothing illegal (p.551). The design does not establish that the label operates through quid pro quo rather than the other mechanisms listed under theory.
extraction.scope: Population: U.S. House offices of one party that had not cosponsored one bill, one advocacy group, one set of meetings. Institution: House district offices and their schedulers, not Senate or committee-level access. Era: 2013, after Citizens United (2010); the paper frames findings against Citizens United and McCutcheon v. FEC (p.556). Generalization to corporate or wealthy donors and to other contexts is explicitly untested (p.555).

limitations: One experiment cannot establish which mechanism (quid pro quo, expected future donations, expertise, preference intensity, prognostic value of donors) produces the effect; the authors call mechanism 'ripe for future research' (p.555).

summary_md:
Kalla and Broockman ran a blocked randomized field experiment in 2013. CREDO Action asked 191 House offices for a district meeting about a chemical-ban bill. All offices belonged to one party and none had cosponsored the bill. In one office per covariate-matched triplet (64 offices, a number derived from the design), the request called the attendees "local campaign donors". The other 127 offices were told "local constituents", and nothing else changed. The outcome was the rank of the most senior official who attended. Over June to August 2013, a chief of staff or more senior official attended in 12.5% of donor-label offices and 2.4% of constituent-label offices (p=.006). For legislative director or above the figures were 18.8% and 5.5% (p=.005), and for the Member personally 7.8% and 2.4% (p=.07). Lower-ranked staff showed no reliable difference (48.4% vs 43.3% at any district staffer or above, p=.26). The ordered probit gave p=.05.

The randomized treatment was the donor label, not real money. The paper cannot say why the label works, and it measures access, not influence. Only 9 offices cosponsored during the study, so the cosponsorship comparison tells us nothing.

For Paul's systems, the paper mainly bounds an existing citation. flip_model.py:21 cites Kalla and Broockman for "money buys access/effort > votes" and labels the 0.35/0.65 money/peer split CALIBRATED. The paper supports the access half of that line. It says nothing about votes, positions, cosponsorship or the money-to-peer ratio, so it cannot calibrate those constants.

The paper's best transferable idea is its outcome measure: the seniority of the official who takes the meeting. The prospective contract and the staffer routes have no outcome of that kind. The contract scores new cosponsorships, which is the same low-base-rate outcome that left this paper uninformative. Nothing here supports the competitiveness multiplier.

Repatriation identification: Lexis-Nexis 10-K search for "repat!" within 50 words of AJCA, Homeland Investment, or HIA; 1,350 candidate firms. Group 1 (repatriated): 476 firms; amounts available for 450 (443 exact, 7 estimated from tax benefits), totaling $298.36bn. Group 2 (declined): 647. Group 3 (considered, then silent): 227. Compustat FY2004 covers 466 repatriators and 774 non-repatriators (p.19). Lobbying data: hand-collected from Senate LDA semi-annual filings (sopr.senate.gov), FEC, CapitalEye.org, and annual reports. Lobbying-firm sample N = 93 (39 coalition, 54 non-coalition). IRS SOI benchmark: 843 of about 9,700 eligible corporations (p.15).
extraction.method: (1) Descriptive comparison of repatriating vs non-repatriating firms: means and medians with significance tests (Table 1). (2) Industry tabulation by one-digit and two-digit SIC (Table 2). (3) Logistic regression of a repatriation indicator on ln(total assets), cash/assets, liabilities/assets, pre-tax income indicator, operating cash flow/sales, and industry dummies (Table 3). (4) OLS of ln(amount repatriated) on the same regressors, N = 434, adjusted R2 = .48 (Table 5, fn 91). (5) Return on lobbying = estimated tax savings / estimated lobbying expense, with savings = amount repatriated x 35% x 85% (Table 6, Sec. III.B.2). Also a subsample of 48 firms spending over $1M.
extraction.identification: No causal identification design. The authors exploit the one-year, elective, audited-disclosure tax holiday so that the benefit is observed directly. Comparisons are cross-sectional: no instrument, no difference-in-differences, no pre-period. Lobbying spend is set to an upper bound to avoid overstating ROI (p.28, fn 97). The text does not show the regression with lobbying as a regressor that the introduction describes (p.3).
extraction.scope: US publicly traded firms that filed 10-Ks and disclosed AJCA s.965 repatriations. Institution: the one-time dividends-received deduction, its IRS guidance (Notices 2005-10, 2005-38, 2005-64), and congressional lobbying over it. Era: 2004-2006. Population is limited to firms with material or disclosed repatriation and foreign operations.

key_findings.finding: Estimated return on lobbying for the AJCA repatriation provision is about $220 of tax savings per $1 spent (22,000%). Coalition firms return 257; non-coalition lobbyists 154; per-company average 869; the >$1M subsample 243; per-company median 172.2.
key_findings.numbers: Overall ROI 220; savings $62.05bn (46,157.5 + 15,897.0) on $282.7M lobbying; coalition ROI 257; non-coalition 154; mean per-company 869; >$1M subsample 243

key_findings.finding: The 93 lobbying firms repatriated about 70% of total dollars. Coalition members (39) repatriated 52% of total dollars, and non-coalition lobbyists (54) 18%. Non-lobbying firms (357, 80% of repatriators) account for 30%.
key_findings.numbers: Lobbyists $209.1bn of $298.36bn; coalition $155.7bn; non-coalition $53.4bn; non-lobbying $89.3bn; average lobbyist spend $3.0M, range $10,000 to $24.7M (GE)

key_findings.finding: Repatriating firms are much larger, more profitable, and hold less cash than non-repatriating firms. Medians differ significantly on assets, cash ratio, leverage, pre-tax margin, and operating cash flow.
key_findings.numbers: Mean assets $24,833M vs $6,703M; median $2,511M vs $570M; mean cash/assets 15% vs 20%; percent profitable 91% vs 75%; mean pre-tax income/revenue 12% vs -32%

key_findings.finding: Logit: repatriation decision is predicted by size, profitability indicator, and operating cash flow. Cash and leverage are not significant. Industry dummies are not significant.
key_findings.numbers: ln assets .415 (p<.001); pre-tax income indicator .729 (p=.001); OCF/sales 1.918 (p<.001); cash/assets .225 (p=.640); liabilities/assets -.409 (p=.269); logit N not reported

key_findings.finding: OLS on amount repatriated (N=434, adj R2 .48): size, cash ratio, and cash flow are significant, but pre-tax profitability is not.
key_findings.numbers: ln total assets .915 (p<.001); cash/assets 3.702 (p<.001); OCF/sales 1.679 (p=.023); liabilities/assets 1.186 (p=.085); pre-tax income indicator -.314 (p=.330); SIC 3800 indicator 2.196 (p=.085)

key_findings.finding: Repatriation dollars are concentrated in pharmaceutical and manufacturing firms. SIC 2830 (drugs) accounts for $96bn from 26 firms, 63% of SIC 2000 totals. Average repatriation per firm is $663M, about 8% of assets.
key_findings.numbers: Total $298,360M across 450 firms; SIC 2000 more than half of dollars; SIC 2830 $96bn; SIC 3600 $22.5bn from 44 firms

key_findings.finding: Disclosing firms are 56% of the IRS's 843 repatriating corporations but over 95% of dollars.
key_findings.numbers: 476 firms vs 843; $298bn vs $312bn qualifying

key_findings.finding: The authors find no evidence that the repatriation produced job growth. ASA and BLS data show no 2005 employment spike. The Sinai 660,000-job projection cited by supporters is treated as unsupported.
key_findings.numbers: Sinai projection $265-406bn repatriation and 660,000 jobs; ASA buybacks S&P 500 $169bn (2004) to $334bn (2005)

key_findings.finding: Internal inconsistency on cash. The abstract and conclusion say cash on hand is not associated with the repatriation amount. Table 5 shows cash/assets significant at p<.001 for amount. The abstract also says industry and size are 'most predictive', but no industry dummy is significant in Table 3 and only SIC 3800 is close in Table 5 (p=.085).
key_findings.location: Abstract (p.1); Sec. IV (p.31); Table 5 (p.26); Table 3 text (p.23)
key_findings.numbers: cash/assets 3.702 p<.001 (Table 5) vs claim of no association (p.1, p.31); SIC 3800 p=.085

key_findings.finding: Policy conclusion: tax benefits went to older, larger, declining firms. The authors argue another repatriation holiday is highly questionable and that lobbying returns of this size question firms' acceptable-return logic.
key_findings.numbers: n/a (qualitative)

limitations: Lobbying expense is an upper bound. Most firms do not report AJCA-specific spend, so the authors use the broadest coded lobbying total (fn 97, p.28). ROI is therefore conservative but not an exact measure of AJCA spend.
Savings assume a 35% marginal rate times 85% deduction (fn 6, pp.29-30), because few firms quantify the benefit. Disclosed benefit definitions vary (fn 81).
ROI is driven by outliers: some firms spending very little returned over $13,000 per dollar (p.30). The authors add a >$1M subsample (48 firms, ROI 243). Mean and median ROI both reported.
Support classification is uncertain for five lobbying firms. Excluding them raises ROI to 228:1 (fn 100, p.30). Five firms that lobbied against the AJCA are excluded (fn 99, p.28).
Non-disclosure: Group 3 firms (227) are assumed to have not repatriated or to have repatriated immaterial amounts (p.19). Repatriators below disclosure thresholds are unobserved (fn 10, p.3).
Measurement of repatriation relies on the 'repat!' keyword search within 50 words of AJCA terms (p.18). Recall of this search is not validated.

No causal design. Cross-sectional correlations only. The text does not show the regression with lobbying as a regressor, which the introduction says exists (p.3). The only lobbying test is the group comparison in Table 6.
Logit sample size is not stated. OLS uses ln transforms for amount, assets, leverage and OCF on an ad hoc basis (fn 91), with N=434.

Internal numeric discrepancies: introduction gives $62.5bn savings and $208bn repatriated by lobbyists (p.3); Table 6 implies $62.05bn and $209.1bn. Introduction gives 496 repatriating firms vs 476 elsewhere (p.3 vs p.18).
Single tax holiday in one era. External validity to other lobbying or tax provisions is limited. The authors' planned follow-up on the second repatriation holiday is not in the text (p.32).
Draft status: placeholders in the text (e.g., 'Cite updated Sinai study', fn 35; blank citations in fns 24, 36-37, 42, 65). The working paper has not been finalized.
measures: Repatriation indicator (1 if Group 1, from 10-K disclosure).
Amount repatriated (dollars, 10-K disclosure; 7 firms estimated from tax benefits; ln in OLS).
Repatriation as % of total assets (Table 4).
Estimated tax savings = amount repatriated x 35% x 85% (Table 6).
Lobbying expenditure (LDA filings, upper-bound AJCA estimate; coalition-membership dummy).
ROI = estimated tax savings / lobbying expenditure (overall, per-company average, median, >$1M subsample).
Compustat FY2004: ln total assets, cash/assets, liabilities/assets, pre-tax income indicator, operating cash flow/sales, SIC one- and two-digit indicators.
Sales, market value and foreign-to-total sales are tested in fn 88 but not significant.
references_of_note: de Figueiredo, John M. and Brian S. Silverman, 'Academic Earmarks and the Returns to Lobbying,' NBER Working Paper 9064 (2002), fn 3, p.2. The main prior academic lobbying-return study cited; the paper calls prior results inconclusive.
Nixon v. Shrink Missouri Government PAC, 528 U.S. 377 (2000), fn 3, p.2. Public perception that money buys legislative influence.

Graham, Hanlon and Shevlin, 'Barriers to Mobility: The Lockout Effect of U.S. Taxation of Worldwide Company Profits,' SSRN (fn 18, p.6). Survey evidence that about 75% of repatriated funds came from liquid assets.
Dharmapala, Foley and Forbes (2008), 'The Unintended Consequences of the Homeland Investment Act,' fn 68-69, p.15. Each $1 repatriated raised buybacks by about $0.91.
Blouin and Krull (2008), 'Bringing It Home,' fn 68, p.15. Repatriating firms increased repurchases relative to non-repatriators.
Clemens and Kinney (2008), Tax Notes 759, fn 69, p.16. Only significant increase by repatriators was in buybacks.
Redmiles, IRS Statistics of Income Bulletin (2008), fn 64, p.15. IRS study: 843 of about 9,700 eligible corporations repatriated $312bn. Benchmark for the sample.
Kingston, Charles, 'The Great American Jobs Caper,' 58 Tax L. Rev. 327 (2005), fn 15, 56, 60-61. Critical view that the AJCA is political cover.
Sheppard and Sullivan (2009), 'Multinationals Accumulate to Repatriate,' Tax Notes 295, fn 68, p.15-16. Repatriating firms reduced US employment.
Maples and Gravelle, CRS Report (2009), fn 65, p.15. Repatriation increased more than eightfold versus base dividends.

short_quotes.quote: Firms lobbying for the repatriation provision were quite effective in receiving lucrative tax benefits

summary_md:
Alexander, Scholz and Mazza study the one-time dividend repatriation deduction in the 2004 American Jobs Creation Act (s.965). They treat lobbying as an investment and divide estimated tax savings (amount repatriated x 35% x 85%) by each firm's LDA-reported lobbying spend. They used a "repat!" keyword search of 10-Ks for 2004-2006 to identify 476 repatriating firms, with dollar amounts for 450 (total $298bn). 93 of those firms lobbied. The headline ROI is about 220:1 ($62bn of savings on $282.7M of lobbying). Coalition members return 257:1 and solo lobbyists 154:1. Outliers drive the result: the per-company mean is 869:1 and the median 172:1. The lobbying denominator is an upper bound, and the design is purely cross-sectional, with no causal identification. Logit and OLS models (N=434 for the amount) show that size, profitability and operating cash flow predict who repatriated and how much. The abstract and conclusion say cash holdings do not matter, but Table 5 contradicts this (cash/assets 3.70, p<.001).

For Paul's systems this is a firm-side, policy-rent return on lobbying expenditure. It tells us nothing about how legislators respond, and it does not cover PAC contributions. Melange's "ROI" and break-even figures measure expected member flips per PAC dollar, so the 220:1 figure does not transfer to them. The paper does sharpen two points. First, its biggest returns came on an essentially uncontested provision, which bears on the contested-bills design. Second, its upper-bound denominator would double-count in-house and outside-firm LDA dollars that Mentat keeps separate. The paper is UNVERIFIED as a source for any Melange constant.

paul_entries.citation: Alexander, Mazza & Scholz 2009, SSRN lobbying rates of return (AJCA)

bearings.paper_claim: ROI = estimated tax savings / lobbying expense = about 220:1 overall ($62.05bn / $282.7M). Coalition 257, non-coalition 154, per-company mean 869, median 172.2, firms over $1M 243. Unit is the firm, window is FY2004-2006, denominator is the 93 lobbying repatriators.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. III.B.2, Table 6 (pp.28-30); fn 97, fn 100
bearings.system_side: Melange's 'ROI' is desk_roi: the expected weighted flips gained from the next $10k of PAC money on a member. Break-even solves a(CU)/(a(CU)+b(comp)) = pfbase with the saturating receipts-relative PAC money term. Neither one is a firm's policy-rent return on lobbying dollars.
bearings.transfer_conditions: No numeric transfer. The paper's numerator is the firm's tax benefit from a provision, and its denominator is LDA lobbying spend (an upper bound). Melange's numerator is modeled member movement, and its denominator is FEC PAC dollars capped at $10k per candidate. The paper could at most motivate a separate 'policy value at stake' display. Any such display would need the provision's dollar value, which is a one-off audited disclosure available only under a tax holiday. The median (172) is the defensible central figure, not the mean (869).
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-allocation#Break-even CU spend and ROI floor|Break-even CU spend and ROI floor]]

bearings.paper_claim: Lobbying firms captured about 70% of repatriated dollars ($209.1bn of $298.36bn), but the only lobbying test is a group comparison. The regression with lobbying as a regressor that the introduction promises (p.3) is not in the text. No legislator-level outcome is observed.
bearings.paper_location: Table 6 (p.29); p.3; Sec. IV (pp.31-32)
bearings.system_side: pflip treats money as the minority partner (WM 0.35 vs WP 0.65). Its saturating term uses PAC dollars relative to receipts and cites 'money buys access/effort > votes'. The model takes no input from lobbying expenditure.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This does not bear on WM, WP or HALFF. The paper measures what firms got from a provision, not whether any member moved, and it measures lobbying rather than PAC giving (Furnas et al. find low overlap). It gives no grounds to raise the money weight. Paul's 'ROI enthusiasm' finds no legislator-level support here.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-influence-engine#Flip - winnability model|Flip - winnability model]]

bearings.paper_claim: Repatriators are larger and more profitable. Logit: ln assets .415 (p<.001), pre-tax income indicator .729 (p=.001), OCF/sales 1.918 (p<.001). OLS on the amount (N=434, adj R2 .48): ln assets .915, cash/assets 3.702 (p<.001). The 'industry most predictive' claim is unsupported: no industry dummy is significant in the logit, and SIC 3800 has p=.085 in the OLS.
bearings.paper_location: Tables 1, 3, 5 (pp.20-26); abstract p.1 vs Table 5
bearings.system_side: The study regresses sector-year log giving and log lobbying on lagged growth, phase, toss-up and trend, with sector FE and a wild cluster bootstrap. The lobbying series are LDA outside-firm income and self-filer expenses kept separately, with LobbyView undifferentiated sums flagged as double-counting. Results: no stable growth effect, and the lobbying lead flips sign under year FE.
bearings.transfer_conditions: These are firm-level predictors of capturing a benefit, not of lobbying spend. They are weak support for the 'deep pockets' motivation and say nothing about sector-year growth effects. The study's null result is not contradicted. Any firm-size covariate drawn from this paper should be cited as single-era (2004-2006) and cross-sectional.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/mentat-sector-growth-study#Sector growth vs giving, partisan share and lobbying regressions|Sector growth vs giving, partisan share and lobbying regressions]]

bearings.paper_claim: The extreme returns arose on a provision with concentrated benefits and no organized counter-lobby. The authors excluded the 5 firms that lobbied against the AJCA. Coalition lobbyists out-returned solo lobbyists (257 vs 154).
bearings.system_side: A per-bill registry with standard, advisory or contested modes. Contested records supply an explicit counterparty set. The loader is shipped, but no consumer is wired (CONTESTED_V1 is future).
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper implies that return figures from an uncontested provision overstate what to expect where banks and CUs oppose each other. Any ROI or value display should be keyed to the bill's mode. This is a design implication only: the paper never studies contested bills.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-lobbying#Contested-bills registry|Contested-bills registry]]

gaps_exposed: The system has no measure of the policy value at stake per bill or provision (dollar rents). The paper shows this, not legislator movement, is where very large 'returns' appear.
There is no coalition-membership signal for industry actors. The paper reports coalition firms returning 257:1 vs 154:1 for solo lobbyists, without strata or tests.
No component separates uncontested provisions with concentrated benefits from contested bills when interpreting returns. The contested-bills loader exists but has no consumer.
flags: The paper's 220:1 return is a firm-level policy-rent ratio on LDA spend. It must not be relabeled as a return on PAC money or a per-member persuasion rate in Melange's ROI or break-even surfaces.
D-021: the paper uses LDA dollars as an ROI denominator (a weight). Any proposal to import LDA spend as an edge or weight in Melange's engines conflicts with D-021 (LDA is an identity source only).

Denominator hazard: the paper uses the 'broadest coded' lobbying total as an upper bound. Mentat rules keep in-house expenses and outside-firm income separate and never summed (giving_forecast.py:379,554,2074), and sgs_config.R:119 records a 9-26% self-filer double count. A replication must not add the two series.

Quoting rule: the coalition (257) vs non-coalition (154) gap and the 220 headline are pooled over a heavily outlier-driven distribution (mean 869 vs median 172). Quote them with window and denominator (FY2004-2006, 93 lobbying repatriators) and with the median.
Internal inconsistency in the paper: the abstract and conclusion say cash is not associated with the repatriation amount, but Table 5 has cash/assets 3.702, p<.001. Do not cite the abstract's claim.
paul_alignment: Partly aligned. Paul calls the Alexander figure an outlier. The paper agrees: it reports a per-company mean of 869 against a median of 172 and adds a >$1M subsample (243) because tiny spenders reach 13,000:1. His wish to include competing-industry conflict is also reinforced, since the return comes from an essentially unopposed provision. His wider 'lobbying as ROI' framing is not supported at the legislator level. The paper never observes members, so it cannot justify the system moving away from its conservative 'money buys access, not votes' flip model. His note is also stale in one respect: the system's ROI (desk_roi, flips per $10k PAC) and the sector-growth study's null result have since diverged from the firm-rent sense of ROI he took from this paper.

related.why: Also treats firm lobbying as producing returns or rents, and is cited alongside Alexander for the break-even/ROI and growth-study components.
Links corporate lobbying to firm size and market concentration. This parallels Alexander's finding that large, profitable firms captured the repatriation benefit.
Shows low overlap between lobbying and PAC spending. This is why Alexander's lobbying ROI cannot be carried over to Melange's PAC-money flip and break-even terms.
Both rest on LDA filings at the firm level; LobbyView is the processed version of the Senate LDA records Alexander hand-collected.
Reviews empirical lobbying-return designs. It supplies the identification framework that Alexander's cross-sectional ROI lacks.
Reviews coalition lobbying. Alexander's coalition (257) vs non-coalition (154) return gap is an untested data point for it.

meta.title: Evaluating voice samples as a potential source of information about personality
meta.venue: Acta Psychologica 230 (2022) 103740 (open access, CC BY; received 15 Mar 2022, accepted 4 Sep 2022, online 18 Sep 2022)

extraction.title: Evaluating voice samples as a potential source of information about personality
extraction.venue: Acta Psychologica 230 (2022) 103740 (open access, CC BY; received 15 Mar 2022, accepted 4 Sep 2022, online 18 Sep 2022)
extraction.coverage: Full text read: all 1,313 lines of the text file (front matter, abstract, Introduction, Method, Preprocessing, Analytic strategy, Results, Discussion incl. Tables 2 and 3, Conclusion, data availability, CRediT, and references). No section skipped. Page numbers below are the journal's printed page numbers, inferred from the running headers in the text. Metadata hint was correct except for the DOI/article-number details, which are now confirmed from the text. Topic coverage: the paper contains nothing on lobbying, networks, path-finding, allocation, elections, persuasion/turnout, or legislators. Its only relevant area is text measurement (LIWC 2015 linguistic features, pyAudioAnalysis vocal features) and ML prediction methodology, both covered in full. paul_markup: no annotation file exists for this item (checked _annots, _raw, _work and annotations for adbeab3f0b2a; none found), so the list is empty.
extraction.research_question: (1) How much information about personality (Big Five, self-report) is conveyed by the linguistic (LIWC 2015) and vocal (pyAudioAnalysis) features of short, semi-structured voice samples? (2) Do semi-structured voice samples reveal more about some personality traits than others? Secondary benchmarks: depression, age and gender (p.2, lines 148-156; p.4).
extraction.theory: Six potential mechanisms linking voice samples to personality (p.1-2): (1) personality drives what people talk about; (2) personality drives how people talk (e.g., loudness, smoking affecting voice); (3) content of speech affects how others treat the speaker, which affects personality; (4) delivery style affects treatment, which affects personality; (5) and (6) a third variable (education, culture, biology) affects personality and either what is said or how it is said. Background: language-personality links across written and spoken text (Pennebaker et al., 2003; Yarkoni, 2010). Prior voice-personality work used either observer ratings or narrow vocal parameters (p.2). The paper states the mechanisms are not tested (p.7).
extraction.data: Sample: UT Austin Introductory Psychology students in a Synchronous Massive Online Course, Fall 2018 (UT1000 Project). Of 1,342 students who completed a 3-week self-tracking assignment, 1,087 used the smartphone app; 213 (email) and 42 (journal) were excluded because they had no audio (p.2). 992 smartphone students gave 25,163 audio responses (mean 21.32 s; mean 40.28 words) (p.2). Preprocessing kept responses with at least 50 words per Google Speech-to-text, leaving 5,838 responses (p.3). One sample per person was kept (each person's first response with at least 50 words; 64% were their first response) = 614 analytic samples, mean 50.74 s and 92.41 words (SD 73.69) (p.3). Unit of analysis: one voice sample per participant. Table 1 Ns: Extraversion, Conscientiousness, Neuroticism, Openness, Agreeableness 545 each (means ~37-46, alpha 0.76-0.89); Depression 485 (CES-D-10, mean 11.26); Age 564 (mean 18.57, SD 1.34); Gender 564 (Female 374, Male 190) (p.3). The text does not explain why the Ns differ from the 614 analytic samples beyond noting different survey completion times (Table 1 note). Predictors: 94 LIWC 2015 dimensions (p.3) and 272 pyAudioAnalysis vocal features (136 per 1-s segment statistic, mean and SD over 1-s segments) (p.3). Outcomes: BFI-2 (60 items, 5-point scale) at end of week two; CES-D-10 about two weeks after the assignment (p.2). Recording prompt: describe your situation and current thoughts and feelings, plus about 10 s of environmental sound (p.2).
extraction.method: Two-stage, automated machine learning pipeline in R 4.1.2 (mlr 2.19.0, mlrMBO 1.1.5) with XGBoost (1.5.2.1) as the learner (p.3-4). Stage 1 (global search): 150 Latin Hypercube hyperparameter configurations, each scored by 10-fold CV; a Gaussian Process surrogate and CMA-ES then propose new configurations for sequential model-based optimization, run for at least 50 cycles (extended while improvement continued) (p.4). Feature set fixed at 100%. Stage 2 (feature selection): nested 10-fold CV within each outer fold, Tree SHAP values for each test sample, a pseudo partial R-squared per feature (R-squared of model with the feature's SHAP removed vs. full model), repeated five times and weighted by error; top-30 features kept per outer fold and XGBoost refit with stage-1 hyperparameters held fixed; performance is the mean over the 10 outer folds (p.4). Evaluation: out-of-sample R-squared for regression defined as 1 minus CV test MSE divided by outcome variance (p.4). For classification, log loss is used rather than AUC, and scored as 1 minus model log loss over intercept-only log loss (p.5). Uncertainty: no standard test fits the repeated selection, so final models were re-estimated with 100-fold CV (about 9% more training data per fold), on the assumption that a generalizable model improves with more data (p.5). Post-hoc: reliability (Cronbach alpha, mean feature test-retest correlation) used to disattenuate performance (Spearman 1961) and to test whether scale reliability predicts model performance (p.7-8).
extraction.identification: None causal. The design is cross-validated out-of-sample prediction only; the authors state that without an experimental design the causal direction of each mechanism cannot be established and most variables cannot be manipulated (p.7, lines 907-913). The generalizability standard is that a model fitted on some people predicts unseen people's self-reported traits from voice data (p.9).
extraction.scope: Population: UT Austin Introductory Psychology students who used a smartphone app (mean age 18.6; 374 female, 190 male in the gender analysis), with self-report personality, depression, age and gender. Era: data collected Fall 2018, published 2022. Context: one standardized, open-ended voice prompt with mixed content and environments (not a lab reading task). The paper does not state the speech language or dialect. Results are described as a conservative estimate for brief (about 92 words), constrained, student-only samples (p.8).

key_findings.finding: Voice samples (joint LIWC + vocal features) explained 10.67% of variance in personality traits on average; LIWC alone 3.13%; vocal alone 6.24%.
key_findings.numbers: joint 10.67%, vocal 6.24%, LIWC 3.13% (average across Big Five traits, out-of-sample R-squared, 100-fold CV)

key_findings.finding: Up to about 16% of trait variance was explained, mainly for Extraversion, Conscientiousness, Neuroticism and Agreeableness.
key_findings.numbers: up to 16%; joint-set models for E, C, N in the 10-20% range; single feature sets under 10%

key_findings.finding: Openness was the least well predicted trait (under 10% variance). Agreeableness and Openness were the two least well predicted traits in the discussion.
key_findings.location: Results p.5, lines 575-577; Discussion p.7, lines 849-852
key_findings.numbers: Openness below 10%

key_findings.finding: Depression was predicted at 11-18% of variance, and gender at over 90%. Vocal features predicted gender almost perfectly.
key_findings.location: Results p.5, lines 577-579; Discussion p.8, lines 1009-1013
key_findings.numbers: depression 11-18%; gender over 90%; depression mean 11.26 (CES-D-10, N=485)

key_findings.finding: Joint features beat single feature sets for all traits except Agreeableness (best with vocal features only). Gender was the other task where joint features were not best.
key_findings.location: Results p.5-6, lines 580-582, 614-616; Conclusion p.9, lines 1168-1171
key_findings.numbers: exception: Agreeableness (vocal-only best) and gender

key_findings.finding: Neuroticism was predicted better by linguistic features than by vocal features. Extraversion, Conscientiousness and Neuroticism were the traits where the joint set reached 10-20%.
key_findings.location: Results p.5, lines 583-595; Discussion p.8-9, lines 1014-1019
key_findings.numbers: E, C, N joint 10-20%; single sets under 10%

key_findings.finding: Joint-feature performance was more than the sum of the separate feature sets, which the authors read as an interaction between language and voice.
key_findings.location: Results p.6, lines 606-608; Discussion p.6-7, lines 662-670; Conclusion p.9, lines 1176-1181
key_findings.numbers: joint performance exceeded sum of LIWC and vocal performance

key_findings.finding: Top LIWC predictors: negate (Extraversion), pronoun (Conscientiousness), Analytic/Tone (Neuroticism). Top features are mostly vocal (MFCC, chroma, spectral entropy, delta features), not pitch or loudness. Feature rankings are reported as hard to interpret.
key_findings.numbers: top-5 features per condition in Table 2; features ordered by pseudo partial R-squared

key_findings.finding: Post-hoc: the reliability-prediction correlation was t(4)=2.65, r=0.80, p=.057, but leave-one-out CV gave r=0.309, so the true association is much smaller. Reliability did not change the ordering of traits.
key_findings.location: Post-hoc p.7, lines 930-935; Table 3 and text p.8, lines 944-954

key_findings.finding: Disattenuated (reliability-corrected) out-of-sample R-squared roughly tripled to quadrupled; the ordering of traits stayed the same. Original to disattenuated: E 0.16 to 0.57; C 0.11 to 0.47; N 0.15 to 0.56; O 0.04 to 0.17; A 0.07 to 0.26; depression 0.18 to 0.67.
Sample reduction and sample size: 25,163 responses reduced to 5,838 with at least 50 words, then to 614 (one per person). Mean word count of final samples 92.41.
Model-based uncertainty: 100-fold CV improved out-of-sample R-squared by about 4% on average (gender by about 1.5%).
key_findings.numbers: approximately 4 percentage points on average; gender about 1.5%

limitations: Samples were brief (mean about 92 words), collected in a constrained context (a class-assignment prompt), and drawn from Introductory Psychology students; the authors call the results a conservative estimate (p.8, lines 1031-1041).
The criterion was self-report Big Five scores, which the authors acknowledge have their own biases; they call for non-self-report validation (p.8, lines 1049-1055).
The 50-word threshold is acknowledged as arbitrary; it was set from a Reddit study (25 words) and doubled (p.3, lines 237-243).

Two-stage modeling: hyperparameters tuned on 100% of features were reused after selecting the top 30, which the authors say may be suboptimal. This likely explains why the joint set underperformed vocal-only for Agreeableness (p.9, lines 1108-1135).
No pooling across tasks: predicted gender, age or depression were not used as features for personality prediction (p.9, lines 1136-1149).
No standard statistical test fits the repeated model and feature selection; the uncertainty approach relies on an untested assumption about 100-fold CV (p.5, lines 528-557).

Feature-level interpretation is heavily caveated: many features, non-monotonic effects, and variance explained is not the same as importance (p.6, lines 631-641). The explanations offered for feature-trait links are described as highly speculative (p.8, lines 1020-1022).
Post-hoc reliability correlation (r=0.80, p=.057) is not robust under leave-one-out (r=0.309) (p.7).
No causal identification and no experimental design; mechanisms in the Introduction were not tested (p.7, lines 907-913).
Ns differ across outcomes (Table 1 note: 545 for Big Five, 485 for depression, 564 for age and gender); the text does not fully reconcile these with the 614 analytic samples (p.3).

Raw voice data may contain personally identifiable information; the authors offer analyses or anonymized features on request (p.9, lines 1191-1194). Supplementary files: FeatureRankings.csv, SHAP_Data.RDS, SHAP_Indicators.RDS (p.6).
measures: Big Five personality: BFI-2 60-item (Soto & John, 2017), 5-point agreement scale, reverse items recoded; Cronbach alpha 0.76-0.89 (Table 1)
Depression: CES-D-10 (Andresen et al., 1994), 4-point scale, sum score; alpha 0.86
Age (mean 18.57, SD 1.34) and gender (self-reported, 374 female, 190 male)
Linguistic features: LIWC 2015, 94 dimensions (proportion of words per category except analytic thinking, authenticity, clout, emotional tone) (p.3)
Vocal features: pyAudioAnalysis, 272 features per sample from 34 basic audio dimensions over 50 ms and 1 s segments (p.3)

Pseudo partial R-squared per feature from Tree SHAP values (p.4)

summary_md:
Marrero, Gosling, Pennebaker and Harari (2022) took one short smartphone voice sample (mean 92 words, about 51 s) from each of 614 UT Austin intro-psychology students. They used XGBoost with Tree-SHAP feature selection to predict self-reported BFI-2 traits from 94 LIWC-2015 dimensions and 272 pyAudioAnalysis vocal features. The fit metric is out-of-sample R-squared from 100-fold CV, and the paper gives no permutation null. Averaged across the Big Five, the joint feature set explained 10.67% of variance, vocal features alone 6.24% and LIWC alone 3.13%. Extraversion, Conscientiousness and Neuroticism reached 10-20% with the joint set, Openness stayed under 10%, and gender was predicted at over 90%. The authors say the joint result is more than the sum of the two parts, but they give no causal identification and the criterion is self-report.

This paper is not new to the system. It was the stated method source for `big5_audio_faithful_prereg.md` and was cited in Addendum 1 of `big5_audio_prereg.md`. In July 2026 Melange ran three one-look audio tests at N=90 legislators. Two findings partly carried over: a full eGeMAPS-88 ridge predicted Pink-E (held-out r +0.284, perm-p .030) and Pink-ES (r +0.298, perm-p .017). The paper's headline did not carry over. Super-additivity missed every time: vocal added +0.001 over linguistic for E against Pink, and -0.004 over text against behavioural visibility. Voice did not measure C (r -0.081). The A-ES halo got worse (|r| 0.819 and 0.946).

What the paper means for the system as built: it is the benchmark the audio lane has already tested and largely failed to reproduce in legislators. It explains why audio is display-only, and it does not support moving audio into the engine. Two leads remain open. Its top features (MFCC, chroma, spectral entropy, deltas) are mostly missing from eGeMAPS-88. It also shows reliability disattenuation, which the system never applies to its validity coefficients.

bearings.paper_claim: Vocal features (pyAudioAnalysis, 272) explain 6.24% of variance in self-reported Big Five on average, LIWC 3.13%, and the joint set 10.67%. The authors say the joint result is super-additive (more than the sum of the parts). Extraversion, Conscientiousness and Neuroticism reach 10-20% with the joint set.
bearings.paper_location: Abstract p.1; Results p.5-6 (lines 568-608); Conclusion p.9 (lines 1176-1181)
bearings.system_side: The audio lane designed its 'FAITHFUL Marrero-style replication' around this paper, using vocal, linguistic and joint blocks with ridge, repeated CV and a permutation null at N=90. One-look results: vocal-88 predicts Pink-E (r +0.284, perm-p .030) and Pink-ES (r +0.298, perm-p .017); A, C and O are null. Super-additivity MISSED (+0.001 for E). An earlier pilot against behavioural visibility gave delta -0.004, recorded as 'audio adds NOTHING incremental'. A later test of voice against diligence also MISSED (r -0.081). Audio stays off-chain and display-only.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's criterion is self-report BFI-2 from 18-year-old students, each giving one prompted smartphone sample. The system's criterion is Pink, an LLM text read with reliability about .67 that shares method with the linguistic block, or a behavioural proxy. Its audio is edited broadcast and floor speech from 90 legislators, with venue and channel uncontrolled. The partial replication (vocal carries the arousal traits E and ES) carries over. Super-additivity has not carried over in three looks; the system's own record says it 'did not transfer to our behavioral criterion / legislators'. The paper's metric (out-of-sample R-squared) is not the system's metric (held-out r), so the numbers are only roughly comparable.

The active profile uses only within-speaker F0 deviations and bans cross-speaker absolute F0. A Salam-style sex-cleanliness check showed pace and volume_dynamics are sex-clean.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Carries over directly: sex is acoustically near-deterministic in any adult speech corpus, so any between-member vocal trait score must be sex-conditioned. The paper itself did not control for gender, so the system's handling is stricter than its source.

bearings.paper_claim: LIWC-2015 closed-vocabulary features alone explained only 3.13% of self-reported Big Five variance from samples of about 92 words. The authors call this a conservative estimate driven by short samples. The top LIWC predictors were negate (E), pronoun (C) and Analytic/Tone (N), and feature-level interpretation is 'highly speculative'.
bearings.paper_location: Results p.5 (lines 568-571); Table 2 p.6-7; Discussion p.8 (lines 1020-1041)
bearings.system_side: Builds corpus-relative Big Five from LIWC-analog per-1000-word rates combined with fixed published-correlate weights, then SMOreg/RKH refits. Members below 1500 tokens are flagged lowconf and shrunk toward 0. Held-out CV against RKH ranges from .21 (O) to .51 (E), and the RKH criterion shares method with the text measure.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Partly. Melange corpora are thousands of words per member, not 92, so the paper's small-sample penalty applies only to thin-corpus members, which supports the 1500-token shrinkage floor. The paper's low LIWC-alone figure comes from a self-report criterion in students and says nothing about legislator criteria. Its fixed-feature result does not validate the system's fixed signed weights, because the paper's model is non-linear and re-selects features in each fold.

bearings.system_side: affective_n is an E-residualized, party-controlled LLM affective-facet score. A LIWC-style i + negemo - posemo index serves only as the convergent anchor (r +.24). Moving N to other genres FAILED (rho .050 and .161), and the voice-ES look is spent.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Weak. The paper supports text over voice for N in self-reported students, which fits the system's text-based N slot. The system's later faithful audio test, however, found vocal-ES carries signal (r +0.298 against Pink). The paper's top N predictors (Analytic, Tone) differ from the system's anchor words (i, negemo, posemo), so it does not validate the specific anchor index.

bearings.paper_claim: No standard test fits the repeated feature selection, so uncertainty was handled by refitting with 100-fold CV on the untested assumption that a generalizable model improves with more data. There is no permutation null. A post-hoc reliability-performance correlation of r=.80 (p=.057) fell to .309 under leave-one-out.
bearings.paper_location: Method p.5 (lines 528-557); Post-hoc p.7-8 (lines 930-954)
bearings.system_side: The audio prereg used Marrero's effect size (r about .25-.33) to set the expected signal. It then found that at N=40 with 88 features the permutation 95th percentile was +0.267, above the locked +0.15 bar. N was raised to at least 80 and a permutation-significance gate was added before the look. That gate stopped audio-E r +0.228 (null +0.234) from passing.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Carries over as a caution. Effect sizes from this paper have no null distribution and come from N=545 self-report, so they should not set a pass bar for an N=90, 88-feature legislator design without a permutation floor. The system's discipline is already stricter than its source.

gaps_exposed: The paper's top-ranked vocal features (MFCCs, chroma, spectral entropy, delta features) are mostly missing from eGeMAPS v02-88. eGeMAPS has only MFCC1-4 and no chroma, and the round-2 prereg names an MFCC route as untried. Any future audio look could only use a richer feature set if it is pre-registered and kept to a single look, and it would stay UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

Disattenuation: the paper shows reliability-corrected out-of-sample R-squared roughly triples (E 0.16 to 0.57). The system reports validity coefficients against Pink (reliability about .67) and RKH but does not correct them, and attenuation is mentioned only in prose.

There is no self-report or observer personality criterion for legislators, so a Marrero-faithful self-report replication cannot be run. Pink is the stand-in criterion, and it shares method with the linguistic block, which biases the super-additivity bar against vocal features.

Venue and editing confound: the paper used one unedited smartphone sample per person. The system pools edited broadcast and floor audio with venue effects (disfluency about 26 per 1k words live vs 0.22 on NPR), and that variance is not modelled in the trait tests.

Nothing in the paper, or in the system's audio results, links voice-derived traits to legislative behaviour or lobbying responsiveness. Even if voice measured traits, that would not support feeding them into the receptivity layer.
flags: Do not cite this paper as support for voice adding to text in legislators. Super-additivity MISSED in all three Melange looks (+0.001 against Pink-E, -0.004 against visibility, -0.046 for C), and the system's own record says the paper's super-additivity 'did not transfer'. The single exception is exploratory, not confirmatory: vocal added +0.119 for E against behavioural visibility in round 2. It stays UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

Addendum 1 of big5_audio_prereg.md (line 87) reads the paper as showing 'A carried MORE by voice than text = halo-relevant'. The authors attribute Agreeableness doing best with vocal-only features to hyperparameters tuned on the full feature set being reused after selection, which they call likely suboptimal (p.9, lines 1108-1135). That reading over-states the paper and should not be repeated.

Metric mismatch: the paper reports out-of-sample R-squared (1 - CV MSE / variance); Melange reports held-out correlation r. Converting the paper's 6-16% to r of about .25-.40 as an 'expected effect' is approximate, and any comparison should name both metrics and their denominators (N=545 self-report students vs N=90 legislators against Pink).
No conflict with D-025, D-021, the rejected SNA proposals or the reciprocity rulings: the paper has no network, lobbying or edge content.
paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this paper. His recorded interest is in non-text channels (audio, video), and his position under prosody-and-disfluency is that 'the system concluded audio is display-only'. The evidence agrees with that conclusion. The paper is optimistic about voice, but in Paul's own replications (he supplied the paper in July 2026, per Addendum 1) only the arousal-trait signal carried over. The super-additivity that would make voice worth adding did not. His note is not stale, but it is thinner than the record: it does not mention that the faithful replication validated vocal E/ES against Pink, or that three super-additivity tests and the halo attack all MISSED. Read together with Simchon, the paper was framed as the case for making psychology load-bearing 'IF the pilot proves fruitful'. The pilot did not prove fruitful for that purpose, so that conditional should be treated as closed.

The congressional pitch method that replaced trait inference in the active audio profile, as within-speaker topic-conditioned F0 (Addendum 6). It is the domain-specific alternative to Marrero's student self-report design.
Audio-as-data pitfalls (alignment, features, classifiers) bear directly on why Marrero's controlled smartphone result did not carry over to edited political audio.
A meta-analysis of LIWC-Big Five links that puts Marrero's LIWC-only 3.13% in context and bears on the lexical-big5 instrument's closed-vocabulary weights.
Marrero's theoretical basis for links between language and personality. It is also the source of the system's first-person and negative-emotion anchor for affective-N.
The BFI-2 is Marrero's criterion instrument. No such self-report exists for legislators, which is why Pink stood in.
Text-based elite personality from speech, the legislator-side basis of the lexical-big5 instrument that Marrero's linguistic block parallels in students.
